title: Not a Planet
caption: The planetary nebula PN M 2-53, imaged by the Gemini North telescope
celestial: PN M 2-53 · constellation Lacerta · about 12000 light-years away (source figure)
credit: International Gemini Observatory/NOIRLab/NSF/AURA · Acknowledgements: PI: Rafael Andrés Pignata (Universidad Nacional de Córdoba). Image processing: T. A. Rector (University of Alaska Anchorage/NSF NOIRLab), J. Miller (Gemini Observatory/NSF NOIRLab), M. Zamani & D. de Martin (NSF NOIRLab)

recognition.text: NOIRLab Image of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: Like an inky patch of space smudged by a giant thumbprint, this image shows PN M 2-53, a planetary nebula about 12000 light-years away in the direction of Lacerta. It was captured by Gemini North, one of the international Gemini Observatory's two telescopes.

The name 'planetary nebula' is thoroughly misleading: these objects have nothing to do with planets, or even with exoplanets. The term goes back to the late 1700s, when astronomers thought the glowing gas shapes looked like planets. Wrong as it is, the name has stuck.

In reality, planetary nebulae come from some dying stars at the very end of their lives. The stars shed layers of gas and dust, which are then lit up by the cores left behind. This image was made through filters for oxygen, sulfur and hydrogen-alpha, each capturing the glow of a particular gas in the shell.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (2.77 x 2.21 arcminutes) and distance (12000 light years), the frame spans roughly 9.7 × 7.7 light-years. Its light set out about 12,000 years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: Taken in visible light with the Gemini Multi-Object Spectrograph on Gemini North through [O III], S II and hydrogen-alpha filters; the colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: Narrow filters isolate the glow of particular gases, and the long exposure gathers far more light than the eye could.
